system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-01-17 20:34:00 to 2169-01-19 18:17:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of a persistent headache lasting three weeks, associated with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, and transient visual disturbances. A non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial pathology, supporting a diagnosis of migraine rather than structural or infectious causes. She was unable to take her usual migraine medication, Imitrex, due to interactions with her HIV regimen. During the admission, she was treated for an asymptomatic urinary tract infection with ciprofloxacin and started on lisinopril for newly detected hypertension. Her HIV remained well controlled, and other chronic conditions were managed without change. She was discharged home in good condition with instructions to follow up with her primary care provider and neurology for ongoing headache management.

Osteoarthrosis, localized, not specified whether primary or secondary, lower leg
Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status

radiology_notes.text:
LEFT KNEE RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___.

Comparison is made with a prior study from ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with knee injury.  Evaluate for fracture
or dislocation.

FINDINGS:  AP, oblique, and lateral views of the left knee are obtained.
Evaluation is quite limited due to underpenetrated technique and large body
habitus.  There is a lucent defect along the lateral tibial plateau, best seen
on the AP projection.  Findings may be compatible with acute fracture.  There
is likely a joint effusion though the lateral view is quite limited.

IMPRESSION:

Extremely limited study with concern for lateral tibial plateau fracture.
Recommend CT to further assess given poor technique and large body habitus.

EXAMINATION:  CT left knee.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images of left knee were obtained without intravenous
contrast, with selective sagittal and coronal images.  No priors for
comparison.

HISTORY:  Evaluate for knee fracture.

FINDINGS:  There is a fracture of the medial tibial plateau, which proximally
involves 35 mm x 26 mm of the medial tibial plateau articular surface.  There
is mild displacement of about 2 mm.  In addition, there is very mild medial
side displacement of the plateau fracture fragment.

Incidentally noted are degenerative changes in the knee joint, which include
tricompartmental spurring.  There is a corticated ossific body in the
posterior aspect of the knee joint which likely represents a loose body. 
There is a large joint effusion noted.

IMPRESSION:

Medial tibial plateau fracture.  This finding was conveyed to the referring
physician by the ___ resident.

Degenerative changes.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with fever.  Evaluate for pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  Multiple chest radiographs, most recent of ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Portable AP view of the chest.

FINDINGS:  The right costophrenic angle is cut off from view.  The study is
limited by motion artifact and by body habitus.  Linear atelectasis is seen at
the left lower lobe.  Otherwise, the lungs appear clear with no evidence of
pneumonia.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal limits,
unchanged.  The aorta is tortuous.  Again noted are fixation screws and plate
in the right humerus.

IMPRESSION:  Linear atelectasis at the left lower lobe.  No evidence of
pneumonia.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you while you're here. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I fell at home yesterday. I tripped and landed hard on my left knee. It hurt right away and I couldn’t stand on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you hear a pop or feel any instability in the knee?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pop, but it swelled up fast and it’s been really stiff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve ordered X-rays and a CT scan to get a better look. Given your medical history, we need to be careful about treatment options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got a lot of health issues, yeah. Heart, lungs, HIV, and my weight—I know surgery’s risky for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re leaning toward non-surgical treatment unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. You have a fracture in the medial part of your left tibial plateau. It’s mild—about 2 mm of displacement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not the worst kind. Because the displacement is small and you have other health risks, we’re going to treat this without surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no operation? How will it heal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll wear a hinged knee brace at all times—except when showering—and you must keep your leg non-weight-bearing. That means no putting weight on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No walking on it. What about pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage that. You’re already on methadone for pain, so we’ll keep that and add hydromorphone for breakthrough pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. What about my other meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed everything. Your HIV meds—atazanavir and emtricitabine-tenofovir—are continuing. Your CD4 is good and viral load is undetectable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been stable for years. What about my heart and breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is stable—EF 60%, no acute issues. For asthma, we’re keeping your albuterol and ipratropium. The chest X-ray showed some atelectasis but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Just need to breathe deep. Any infection risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked blood cultures twice—both came back negative. No sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had VRE before after back surgery—don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that and will avoid antibiotics unless needed. But we did find nitrite-positive bacteria in your urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another UTI? Even if I don’t feel it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, asymptomatic. But given your history of kidney stones and past UTIs, we’re treating it with ciprofloxacin for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember taking that last time. Should be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I took hydromorphone last night and slept okay. Knee’s still stiff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The brace helps protect the fracture while it heals. Physical therapy will guide your movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I start PT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll begin in rehab. You’re being transferred to an extended care facility tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need help with mobility and to stay non-weight-bearing. Rehab will provide therapy and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Less than 30 days. They’ll work on range of motion and strength once it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go to rehab tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What meds am I taking home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds continue. Plus hydromorphone for pain, acetaminophen, and ciprofloxacin for the UTI. We’re also adding stool softeners—docusate and bisacodyl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need those—methadone and pain meds constipate me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And remember: brace on at all times, no weight on the leg, and call the clinic if you have increased pain, swelling, or numbness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re signing discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just want to heal safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Keep up with rehab, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see how you’re doing in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after falling at home, resulting in a closed medial tibial plateau fracture. Due to multiple comorbidities including morbid obesity, chronic heart failure, and HIV, surgical intervention was deemed high-risk, so the fracture was managed conservatively with a hinged knee brace and strict non-weight-bearing status. She remained stable throughout the hospitalization, with no complications. An asymptomatic urinary tract infection was treated with ciprofloxacin. Her chronic conditions, including HIV, asthma, and heart failure, were maintained on existing regimens without change. She was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with instructions for continued brace use, pain management, and follow-up care.
